name: Horse chestnut seed extract
short: Injected aescin linked to kidney failure after heart surgery, mostly children (10.7% overall mortality). Extract by mouth: mild, infrequent adverse events (trial reviews). Seed poisoning: case report.
text: For horse chestnut seed extract taken by mouth for chronic venous insufficiency, a Cochrane review of randomised trials found adverse events were usually mild and infrequent and called it efficacious and safe as a short-term treatment, while noting caveats and the need for larger trials; a meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (1,051 patients) and 3 observational studies (10,725 patients) reported no severe adverse events and no significant increase in mild adverse events, and said further studies are needed on long-term safety in routine use. Escins are saponins described as the most active components of horse chestnut seeds, and kidney harm has been reported with aescin (escin) medicines given by injection, a different product and route from the extract taken by mouth; the kidney abstracts do not say which plant their aescin came from. A 1975 single-centre report on a series of patients linked a rise in acute kidney failure after heart surgery, mainly in children aged 2 to 10, to intravenous aescin (39% needed peritoneal dialysis and overall mortality was 10.7%), with no similar case in almost a year after the drug was dropped, whereas a 1976 study of 18 people with normal kidney function given intravenous sodium aescinate for 3 to 6 days found no change in kidney tests, and its authors called for a strict indication in patients with threatening or existing kidney failure. A case report described acute kidney injury in a 58-year-old surgical inpatient that was most likely due to an interaction between sodium aescinate and ginkgo biloba extract; that abstract does not state the route. A review of herb-warfarin interactions lists horse chestnut among herbal products that may potentially increase the risk of bleeding or the effects of warfarin, noting that nearly all such information comes from laboratory data, animal studies or individual case reports. Another case report described painful bruising of the legs in a 23-year-old woman who had started an oral contraceptive and a hair supplement containing Aesculus hippocastanum extract, which the authors call a herbal anticoagulant and a more plausible cause than the contraceptive, which she later resumed alone without reaction. Eating horse chestnut seed, mistaken for edible chestnut, caused epigastric pain, nausea, sweating, mildly raised liver and pancreatic enzymes and atrial fibrillation in a 46-year-old man, which had returned to normal by the next day (case report). The interactions named in the cited sources are ginkgo biloba extract (with sodium aescinate, case report) and warfarin (potential, review).
